question:
A 89-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of bilateral shoulder pain, more severe on the right
side, accompanied by upper arm stiffness and aching. He denies experiencing headache, jaw or arm
claudication, scalp tenderness, or double vision. Physical examination reveals normal temperature and
equal blood pressure readings of 120/80 mm Hg in both arms. Both shoulders demonstrate limited
active and passive range of motion, particularly in external rotation and abduction, with notable crepitus
during movement. Hip range of motion is normal. Temporal arteries are symmetrical without beading or
tenderness, and radial pulses are equal bilaterally. Laboratory testing shows an erythrocyte
sedimentation rate of 25 mm/hr (normal range: 0-17). What is the most appropriate next step in
management? Answer Choices: (A) Initiate prednisone 60 mg daily (B) Order magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) of the cervical spine (C) Perform a temporal artery biopsy (D) Obtain bilateral shoulder
radiographs (E) Initiate prednisone 15 mg daily (F) Prescribe physical therapy for shoulder

impingement (G) Refer for ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injections into both shoulders (H) Obtain a
chest X-ray to rule out paraneoplastic syndrome (I) Initiate nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs) for osteoarthritis (J) Initiate methotrexate therapy for suspected inflammatory arthritis
 A. Obtain a chest X-ray to rule out paraneoplastic syndrome
B. Order magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical spine
C. Initiate prednisone 15 mg daily
D. Prescribe physical therapy for shoulder impingement
E. Initiate prednisone 60 mg daily
F. Refer for ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injections into both shoulders
G. Perform a temporal artery biopsy
H. Obtain bilateral shoulder radiographs
I. Initiate methotrexate therapy for suspected inflammatory arthritis
J. Initiate nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for osteoarthritis
